transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-11-19
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Samir Khan (Aurelia Head of ML), Leah Torres (Product), Victor Ng (SRE), Anya Petrova (Clinical SME)

Summary:
Quick sync on the POC quality evaluation. Reviewed last week's regression where recall dropped on clinical-note prompts after quantization/64-bit kernel switch. Agreed immediate benchmark run on dedicated instance, tightening guardrails on hallucination prompts, and collecting three more labeled prompt sets for evaluation.

Topics:
- Recap of regression: scope & root-cause hypotheses
- Scoring methodology and threshold adjustments (BLEU/ROUGE + domain heuristics + human spot checks)
- Guardrails: prompt-level blocking, model output filters, and red-team examples
- Next steps: bench runs, pricing, and infra constraints for private/dedicated options

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: All right folks, thanks for joining, um we were expecting a short agenda — quick quality review and next steps. Maya, want to start with the regression summary?
[00:18] Maya: Yeah sure. So last week we saw a drop in recall specifically on the clinical-note extraction prompts after we switched the quantization profile to q4_0 on the test instance. The drop is about 8-10 percentage points on exact-match fields — name, medication, dosage. We also saw more hallucinated medication names in free-text fields.
[00:40] Samir: Just to be clear, that was the config you shipped for latency gains right? We pushed q4_0 to try and get tail latency down for the demo.
[00:52] Maya: Correct. The perf looked better, p50 down 30%, p95 down 20%, but the quality trade-off appeared for the discrete extraction tasks. Our hypothesis is kv-cache alignment plus the new kernel path introduces subtle tokenization differences for certain de-identified terms — so it's an edge-case.
[01:14] Leah: We flagged that in the dashboard — the false positive rate jumped, and the QA team saw it in their manual raters. We need a quick mitigation plan because the clinical reviewers won't accept hallucinated meds.
[01:28] Maya: Agreed. Short-term we recommend rolling back that quant profile for the clinical extraction route and instead enable prefix-KV caching plus the tighter stop sequences we discussed. Long-term we're doing a regression run on the dedicated instance with the alternate kernel to reproduce.
[01:44] Jordan: Sounds good. Samir, how important is pushing the dedicated path vs hosted? I remember compliance is a big factor but you also wanted to avoid waiting for infra.
[01:55] Samir: For production, we want dedicated or private. Data residency and audit logs are required by the clinical compliance team. But for the pilot, hosted with stricter retention and VPC peering would be fine — as long as we can reproduce the issue on Dedicated later.
[02:12] Victor: From SRE side, we need details on the peering and egress. If we go private, we have to open specific ports and the firewall team needs exact CIDR ranges. I'll follow up with that list.
[02:25] Jordan: Great — add that as an action item.
[02:29] Maya: Back to scoring: today I ran the automatic eval on 500 labeled samples — balanced across discharge summary, med list, and progress notes. Metrics: exact match for fields dropped from 92% to 84%, F1 down from 0.89 to 0.81. The hallucination detector (heuristic + simple LM likelihood threshold) caught about 60% of the bad outputs.
[02:55] Anya: The heuristic's okay but misses rare drug abbreviations. We need to keep human-in-the-loop for edge cases.
[03:04] Samir: Do we have the diffs per prompt type? It would help to know if it's only medication or also allergy and ICD codes.
[03:11] Maya: Yes — meds and dosage are most affected; allergy extraction looks stable. ICD codes unchanged. I'll upload the per-prompt breakdown to the eval dashboard — link is in the notes.
[03:22] Jordan: Quick question on scoring thresholds — are we comfortable adjusting thresholds for clinical tasks to be more conservative and then tune latency later?
[03:31] Leah: Yes, product prefers false negatives over hallucinations for safety. So higher precision target.
[03:38] Maya: We'll adjust the decision threshold and tighten the hallucination filter. For outputs that don't meet confidence, we'll route to a low-latency fallback model or human review queue.
[03:49] Samir: What's the unit cost if we fallback to a higher-accuracy model for low-confidence items? That affects the economics of the POC.
[03:57] Jordan: I'll share a rough cost estimate in the pricing deck — depends on token volume and the dedicated sizing.
[04:04] Maya: Also, to reproduce we need to run the regression on the same exact model binary on Dedicated — there might be kernel differences between hosted and dedicated builds. I'll schedule a 1k-sample run comparing: hosted q4_0, hosted q4_1, dedicated q4_0 with alternate kernel.
[04:22] Victor: How long for the 1k? If it's batch run on Dedicated we need a window for GPU allocations.
[04:29] Maya: Roughly 30-60 minutes to run and aggregate depending on batching config. We can prioritize it during off-peak.
[04:36] Samir: Can you run the 1k with the same seed/randomization so outputs are deterministic? We need reproducible diffs.
[04:43] Maya: Yep, deterministic sampling with fixed seed. I'll include the raw outputs and the scoring CSV.
[04:49] Jordan: Great. On guardrails, we discussed three levers last week: prompt-level blocking, output filters, and model fallback. Any progress?
[04:58] Maya: Implemented a quick prompt-level blocklist for high-risk trigger phrases and added an output filter that looks for medication patterns and cross-checks against a whitelist. It reduces hallucination by about 40% in the small sample.
[05:12] Anya: Whitelist approach is good but we need frequent updates — drug lists change and local brand names vary. Can we integrate an external med dictionary?
[05:20] Jordan: We can — Redwood supports hooking to customer-provided lists. That would be part of the private deployment integration.
[05:27] Leah: Also need to capture audit logs for any outputs suppressed or escalated. Compliance will want reason codes.
[05:33] Maya: That's on the roadmap — we can emit reason codes and tie them to the eval dashboard.
[05:38] Jordan: Okay good. Any red-team examples to add to regression suite?
[05:42] Samir: I'll send 12 adversarial prompts that caused hallucinations last quarter.
[05:46] Samir: Also, we noticed slightly different tokenization in the transcribed output where hyphenated meds get split which confuses exact-match checks.
[05:54] Maya: Noted — tokenizer normalization step in the post-process can fix many of those exact-match false negatives. We'll add normalization to the scorer.
[06:03] Jordan: Let's talk timeline: Maya runs regression and uploads by Tuesday (2025-11-25), Jordan shares pricing by Friday (2025-11-21), Aurelia provides more prompts by Monday (2025-11-24). Anything else?
[06:14] Victor: I'll confirm firewall/CIDR requirements by 2025-11-26.
[06:18] Maya: We should also run a small A/B with the fallback model to estimate cost delta — maybe 200 samples.
[06:26] Jordan: Put that as a separate mini action.
[06:29] Leah: On the human review queue — if we send 5% of low-confidence items, what's turnaround time? We need SLA for reviewers.
[06:36] Samir: For pilot we can do 4-hour SLA; for prod we'll need 1-2 hour depending on volume.
[06:41] Jordan: Noted.
[06:43] Maya: Any questions about the eval metrics? We're using exact match and F1 for fields, plus LM-based hallucination score and a simple semantic similarity threshold for free-text sections.
[06:55] Anya: For free text we should include a clinical-similarity heuristic not just generic embedding sim — some synonyms are critical.
[07:03] Maya: We can weight clinical token matches higher in the similarity metric.
[07:07] Jordan: All right, let's surface risks: 1) Kernel/quantization leading to subtle token differences; 2) False positives from whitelist gaps; 3) Cost of fallback model. Any mitigation additions?
[07:20] Samir: Add regular sync with clinical team during pilot, maybe weekly spot checks.
[07:25] Leah: And when you do the regression results, flag any prompts where normalization changed the label — want to see pre/post normalization diffs.
[07:33] Maya: Will include pre/post normalization columns in the CSV.
[07:37] Jordan: Cool. Before we wrap, can we agree on the acceptance criteria for the pilot? Samir, Leah — what do you need to sign off?
[07:47] Leah: For product sign-off: precision >= 0.9 on medication extraction and hallucination rate <= 1% on clinical prompts. Also audit logs + suppression reason codes in place.
[07:59] Samir: From ML: reproducible regression run shows no more than 2% delta vs baseline after fixes. From infra: dedicated/private peering confirmed and firewall rules OK.
[08:12] Jordan: Sounds actionable. I'll capture those as acceptance criteria.
[08:18] Maya: I'll start the 1k run after this call and post results.
[08:22] Jordan: Great — recap of next steps in chat. Thanks everyone.
